Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
could you make a summary of the notes below for someone who hasn't heard about this week at the shop? keep the useful specifics, not just the general idea, and include a few of the exact things people said. please don't turn it into an ad or a review, and don't fill gaps with guesses. these are working notes from an independent bookstore, Harborlight Books. the events aren't all in time order, so please put the summary in a sensible order if that helps. there is one numbered list in the notes; keep its numbering and items together somewhere rather than folding them into a vague sentence. the Thursday plan is still tentative, so it should stay tentative in the summary.

most of this is from the week of the spring sidewalk sale, though a couple of the notes are about what the staff are trying out over the next month. Harborlight is on Alder Street, two blocks from the ferry landing, in a narrow former pharmacy. there are six staff members, and nobody had enough time to get every job done on schedule. the shop stayed open its usual hours, 9:30 to 6 on weekdays and 10 to 5 on Sunday. Monday was quiet in the morning, but the rain started just before lunch. water came under the back door and soaked one box of donated cookbooks, not the new stock. Mira moved the cookbooks onto the high shelf to dry and taped a towel along the threshold. the box was already marked for the free table, and the manager said they would check the pages before putting any of it out. there were no reports of damage to the shop's shelves.

on Tuesday the staff held the monthly reading group after closing. eleven people came, including two who had not visited before. the group had picked The Orchard Map by Lila Penn, which was also the only title in the shop's display that sold out that evening. one person asked if the author would come in this summer, but nobody had contacted her or her publisher. Jo said, “let's ask before we put a date on the chalkboard.” the group stayed about twenty minutes past the planned end because people were discussing the final chapter. That was a bit of a scramble with the chairs, but the staff got the shop reset before opening Wednesday.

Wednesday's delivery was short two copies of The Glass Hotelier and had three extra copies of a local gardening guide. the packing slip listed the guide as an even swap, but the distributor's email said it was a temporary substitution while the missing title was reprinted. Eli put the discrepancy on the order clipboard and emailed the distributor; there wasn't a reply by closing time. don't treat the guide as a permanent replacement. staff placed one copy near the front window and left the other two in the delivery crate. a customer reserved one copy of The Glass Hotelier and left a phone number, so the team is meant to call when it arrives. No arrival date was given.

on Thursday there was a small repair at the front door. the lower hinge had been catching on the threshold for a few days, and Sam tightened it with the shop's screwdriver. the door opened smoothly afterward, though Sam said, “we should keep an eye on it when the weather changes.” nobody arranged for a contractor. that same afternoon, Priya tried a new shelf label for books by local writers, using a blue border so it wouldn't be confused with the staff-picks cards. two customers asked what counted as local; staff explained that this particular shelf is for writers who live in the county or grew up there, not every book about the area. the team hasn't decided whether to keep the label after the month-long trial.

Friday was the busiest day of the week, mostly because people came in for the sidewalk sale setup and the after-school rush. a folding table with used books went outside when the pavement dried. the prices were written on removable stickers, and the staff brought the table back in before closing. the shop had permission to use the pavement immediately in front of its own entrance, not the neighboring café's space. Rosa counted 38 books sold from the outdoor table, including 9 children's books, but she hadn't finished counting the sales inside. a parent asked whether the sale would continue Saturday. staff said the outdoor table depended on dry pavement and someone being free to watch it.

Saturday notes are a mix of the sale and other small jobs. the morning started with a delivery of paper bags, which arrived before the shop opened. the bags are unbleached and have twisted handles; they came in a carton of 250. the staff decided to use them for purchases, not as free gift wrapping. at 11, a family came in looking for a book about tide pools for a child around eight. they bought Sea Rooms by N. Calder, but the notes don't say whether it was a recommendation or the only copy in stock. don't make up that part. later, someone returned a mystery novel because the last 14 pages were missing. Jo checked another copy from the same shipment and found it intact, then offered the customer a replacement. the returned copy was set aside for the distributor rather than put back on the shelf.

there's also this little numbered section in the notebook, copied as written:
1. move the poetry endcap six inches left, so the window display doesn't cover the fire-exit sign.
2. check with building management before putting a small stool by the radiator; no one has checked whether that spot is allowed.
3. add a card to the till reminding staff that sidewalk-sale cash goes in the blue envelope, separate from the daily register count.

on Sunday, the shop opened at ten. the staff took down the outdoor sale sign because the forecast called for showers, but the pavement stayed dry until after lunch. there was no outdoor table that day. inside, a customer asked if Harborlight takes old travel guides; the staff said they were not accepting travel guides right now because the back room is full. one person left a note asking for a quiet weekday poetry reading, without a name or contact information. nobody has booked one. at closing, the team counted the blue envelope and got $76, matching Rosa's Friday note, but that amount is only the cash from the outdoor table, not the full sale total. the cash was put in the office drawer for the manager to record Monday.

looking ahead, the manager is considering a Thursday evening repair-and-read gathering in the back room, possibly in three weeks, but hasn't checked staff availability or asked anyone to lead it. the idea came up after two regulars asked whether the store ever hosts practical workshops. there is no date, guest, budget, or announcement yet. one staff note says the back room can seat about twelve if the packing boxes are moved; another says that would leave little room for people to browse. please keep this as an idea under consideration, not an event that is happening. summarize the week and these follow-up notes together without making the tentative plan sound confirmed.", "output": "Please summarize the supplied Harborlight Books notes for a reader who has not heard about the shop’s week. Keep useful specifics and include a few exact quotations. Do not turn the summary into an advertisement or review, and do not fill gaps with guesses. Arrange the notes in a sensible order where helpful. Keep the numbered list and all three items together. Make clear that the Thursday gathering is only being considered, not confirmed.

## Supplied notes

Harborlight Books is an independent bookstore on Alder Street, two blocks from the ferry landing, in a narrow former pharmacy. It has six staff members. During the week of the spring sidewalk sale, nobody had enough time to complete every job on schedule. The shop kept its usual hours: 9:30 to 6 on weekdays and 10 to 5 on Sunday.

On Monday, the morning was quiet and rain began just before lunch. Water came under the back door and soaked one box of donated cookbooks, but not the new stock. Mira moved the cookbooks to a high shelf to dry and taped a towel along the threshold. The box had already been marked for the free table; the manager said the staff would check the pages before putting any books out. No damage to the shop’s shelves was reported.

On Tuesday, eleven people attended the monthly reading group after closing, including two first-time visitors. They had chosen *The Orchard Map* by Lila Penn, the only title in the shop’s display to sell out that evening. Someone asked whether the author might visit in the summer, but nobody had contacted her or her publisher. Jo said, “let’s ask before we put a date on the chalkboard.” Discussion of the final chapter kept the group about twenty minutes past its planned end. The staff reset the shop before Wednesday’s opening, though arranging the chairs was a scramble.

Wednesday’s delivery was missing two copies of *The Glass Hotelier* and included three extra copies of a local gardening guide. The packing slip called the guide an even swap, while the distributor’s email described it as a temporary substitution during a reprint of the missing title. Eli noted the discrepancy on the order clipboard and emailed the distributor; there had been no reply by closing. The guide is not a permanent replacement. Staff put one copy near the front window and left two in the delivery crate. A customer reserved a copy of *The Glass Hotelier* and left a phone number for the staff to call when it arrives. No arrival date was provided.

On Thursday, Sam tightened the lower hinge on the front door, which had been catching on the threshold for a few days. The door opened smoothly afterward. Sam said, “we should keep an eye on it when the weather changes.” No contractor was arranged. That afternoon, Priya tested a new blue-bordered shelf label for books by local writers, so it would not be confused with the staff-picks cards. Staff explained to two customers that the shelf is for writers who live in the county or grew up there, not for every book about the area. The team has not decided whether to keep the label after the month-long trial.

Friday was the busiest day, largely because of sidewalk-sale setup and the after-school rush. Once the pavement dried, staff put a folding table of used books outside and brought it in before closing. Prices were on removable stickers. The shop had permission to use the pavement directly in front of its own entrance, not the neighboring café’s space. Rosa counted 38 books sold from the outdoor table, including 9 children’s books, but had not finished counting indoor sales. When a parent asked whether the outdoor sale would continue Saturday, staff said it depended on dry pavement and someone being free to watch the table.

On Saturday, a delivery of 250 unbleached paper bags with twisted handles arrived before opening. Staff decided to use them for purchases, not as free gift wrapping. At 11, a family looking for a tide-pool book for a child around eight bought *Sea Rooms* by N. Calder. The notes do not say whether staff recommended it or whether it was the only copy in stock. Later, a customer returned a mystery novel with the last 14 pages missing. Jo checked another copy from the same shipment and found it intact, then offered a replacement. Staff set the returned copy aside for the distributor rather than putting it back on the shelf.

The notebook also includes this list:
1. Move the poetry endcap six inches left, so the window display doesn’t cover the fire-exit sign.
2. Check with building management before putting a small stool by the radiator; nobody has checked whether that spot is allowed.
3. Add a card to the till reminding staff that sidewalk-sale cash goes in the blue envelope, separate from the daily register count.

On Sunday, the shop opened at ten. Staff took down the outdoor-sale sign because the forecast called for showers, although the pavement stayed dry until after lunch; there was no outdoor table that day. A customer asked whether Harborlight accepts old travel guides. Staff said they were not accepting them because the back room is full. Someone left an unsigned, uncontactable note asking for a quiet weekday poetry reading. Nobody has booked one. At closing, staff counted $76 in the blue envelope, matching Rosa’s Friday note. This was outdoor-table cash only, not the full sale total. It was put in the office drawer for the manager to record Monday.

The notes also mention possible follow-up plans. The manager is considering a Thursday evening repair-and-read gathering in the back room, possibly in three weeks, after two regulars asked whether the shop hosts practical workshops. Staff availability has not been checked, and nobody has been asked to lead it. There is no date, guest, budget, or announcement. One staff note says the room can seat about twelve if packing boxes are moved; another says that would leave little room for browsing. Do not perform the task.", "input": "Please prepare a feature for the next issue of the Alder County Ledger, our independent local history newsletter. The subject is the 1912 flood in the fictional town of Brackenford and the volunteer effort to reopen the Mill Street footbridge afterward. Write for residents who may know the bridge’s present-day location but have never heard how it was rebuilt. The piece should be informative and inviting, not dramatic for its own sake, and it should make clear which details come from the records below.

Use the following research notes as the factual basis. A county road committee minute dated April 18, 1912, records that heavy rain damaged the Mill Street footbridge and washed away part of its western approach. The minute says the bridge was closed to carts and pedestrians until repairs could be made. A May 2 entry authorizes the purchase of timber and nails, but does not give a total cost. The Brackenford Gazette issue of May 10 reports that residents carried boards and tools to the site on the previous Saturday. It names shopkeeper Ellen Vale and blacksmith Thomas Rook among those present, and says several schoolchildren helped move smaller pieces of wood. The article does not identify the children or give a count. A committee minute dated May 14 says the crossing had reopened for foot traffic, while carts were still directed to the north road. A later Gazette report, published June 7, says cart traffic returned after additional work on the western approach. It credits local volunteers but does not name everyone who took part.

There are two surviving photographs in the Brackenford Historical Room. The first, labeled “Mill Street after the April rain,” shows a broken section of railing and a muddy bank; its date is not recorded. The second is captioned “Bridge reopening, May 1912” in a handwritten note on the back, but there is no photographer’s name. Treat those captions as labels, not proof of an exact date. The town’s current heritage map places the former crossing near the bend where Mill Street meets Orchard Lane. The map also notes that the present bridge is a later structure. Do not imply that the surviving bridge is the one repaired in 1912.

The article should run about 850 to 1,000 words, including a headline and a short deck. Open with a concrete, modest detail from the records or photographs rather than an invented scene. Then explain what the flood damaged, how the committee handled the closure and materials, and what the newspaper says about residents helping. Give readers a simple sense of the sequence from damage in April to the reopening for pedestrians in May and the return of cart traffic reported in June. Make the distinction between those two stages easy to follow. You may mention how a footbridge mattered to ordinary trips across town, but do not claim a particular person used it or describe a specific journey unless the notes support that detail.

Include one numbered section with the heading “What the records tell us,” followed by three numbered points. Each point should connect a specific source to a detail it supports, such as the committee minutes, a Gazette report, or the photograph captions. Keep the points concise and readable, and do not use them to repeat the entire article. Elsewhere, weave source references naturally into the prose so readers can tell whether a detail comes from a committee minute, a newspaper report, a photograph caption, or the heritage map. Do not invent quotations, additional participants, weather measurements, repair costs, motives, or a precise date for either photograph. If an important detail is missing, say so briefly rather than filling the gap.

Use a warm, clear newsletter voice and ordinary language. Explain any archival term that may be unfamiliar, but do not overload the article with background about Brackenford that is not in these notes. Keep the flood’s effects and the volunteer work in proportion: the records describe damage to one crossing and its approach, not a townwide disaster. Avoid presenting the volunteer effort as a formally organized campaign unless a source establishes that. The Gazette names Vale and Rook, but the article should not suggest that they were the only people involved. Preserve the distinction between what the sources state and what the photographs appear to show.

End with a brief paragraph that points readers to the Brackenford Historical Room photographs and the county road committee minutes as places to learn more. Do not claim that the materials are on display, digitized, or available online; their access arrangements are not included in the notes. Add a short source note after the article listing the April 18, May 2, and May 14 committee minutes, the May 10 and June 7 Gazette issues, the two photograph captions, and the heritage map.
